body:
Why is risk assessment needed?

Nanotechnology can provide useful medical, agricultural and industrial applications, but the same physical or chemical properties that make a material useful can also influence its interactions with living organisms.

Risk assessment is the systematic examination of possible harm and the conditions under which that harm may occur. It is different from simply identifying a useful application or confirming that a particle is nanoscale.

Main elements of risk assessment

Hazard identification

The first task is to identify whether the substance could cause adverse effects. Information about the material's composition, physical form and biological effects helps establish the kinds of harm that might occur. Dose-response assessment examines how the likelihood and severity of harm vary with dose.

Exposure assessment

The next task is to determine who or what may come into contact with the material, through which route, and at what level, frequency or duration.

Workers may be exposed during manufacturing; consumers may encounter particular formulations during ordinary use; and organisms may encounter released materials in soil or water.

Risk characterisation

Risk characterisation brings the available hazard and exposure information together to assess the nature and seriousness of potential harm. Uncertainty must be stated when information is incomplete.

Risk assessment is not merely a decision based on particle diameter. For nanomaterials, size distribution, shape, composition, surface properties, solubility and the surrounding medium can all be relevant.

Risk management: preventing exposure

Once a risk is identified, risk management uses appropriate measures to reduce it. A widely applied occupational-safety approach is the hierarchy of controls, which places measures that remove or control hazards at their source above measures that depend mainly on individual behaviour.

  1. Elimination: Remove the hazardous task or material where possible.
  2. Substitution: Replace a hazardous material or process with a safer suitable alternative.
  3. Engineering controls: Use enclosed systems, suitable local ventilation or other physical measures to reduce exposure.
  4. Administrative controls: Establish appropriate work procedures, information, training and restricted access.
  5. Personal protective equipment: Use suitable protective equipment as an additional measure rather than the sole line of protection whenever stronger controls are practicable.

Not every control measure is suitable for every nanomaterial. The choice depends on the substance, the exposure route and the actual work activity.

Safe use throughout a product's life

Safety considerations begin before a nanomaterial reaches consumers. They continue through manufacture, transport, application, maintenance, recycling and disposal.

For example, a nanoparticle safely enclosed inside an intact electronic component may become more available for exposure if that component is mechanically damaged or processed as waste. Thus, use-phase safety does not automatically establish end-of-life safety.

Precaution and scientific uncertainty

A precautionary approach supports reasonable measures to prevent potentially serious harm when scientific information is incomplete. It does not mean that every nanotechnology application must be rejected.

Instead, it encourages reducing avoidable exposure, seeking evidence and reviewing controls when new information becomes available.

In 2017, the World Health Organization issued occupational guidelines for manufactured nanomaterials. The recommendations emphasise preventive exposure control, particularly measures addressing inhalation.

Risk assessment asks what harm may occur and under which exposure conditions. Risk management asks what measures should be used to prevent or reduce that harm.

Prelims focus

  • Risk assessment combines information about hazard and exposure.
  • Risk characterisation considers possible consequences and remaining uncertainty.
  • The occupational hierarchy begins with elimination and substitution before relying on personal protective equipment.
  • Engineering controls act on the source or pathway of exposure.
  • Safety must be considered during manufacture, use and disposal.
  • Trap: Personal protective equipment is not the first or only preferred control measure in the hierarchy.

[Sources: World Health Organization, WHO Guidelines on Protecting Workers from Potential Risks of Manufactured Nanomaterials, 2 February 2017, executive summary and exposure-control recommendations; U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, Hierarchy of Controls, sections on control levels; U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, Nanotechnology Frequently Asked Questions, updated 3 March 2026; sources consulted 13 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Hazard identification and exposure assessment feed risk characterisation; this assessment informs measures to prevent or reduce risk.
pictures.caption: Risk assessment connects hazardous properties, exposure and possible consequences.

pictures.alt: Preferred order: elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, then PPE; source controls precede reliance on behaviour.
pictures.caption: The hierarchy of controls prioritises removing or controlling hazards at their source.

title: Nanomaterial Risk Assessment and Safe Management

body:
Why must the entire life cycle be considered?

A nanomaterial may improve a product's performance during use while creating environmental burdens during raw-material extraction, manufacture or disposal.

For example, a nanostructured coating could reduce the energy needed during the use of a product. But producing that coating may require additional energy, chemicals or processing. Whether the product produces an overall environmental benefit depends on the full comparison.

Life-cycle assessment (LCA) is a systematic method for examining potential environmental impacts associated with the stages of a product's life.

Stages in a nanotechnology product's life

A full product life cycle can include:

  1. Raw-material acquisition: Obtaining the metals, minerals, carbon sources or other substances used in production.
  2. Material and product manufacture: Producing the nanomaterial and incorporating it into a useful product.
  3. Transport and distribution: Moving materials and finished products.
  4. Use and maintenance: Operating the product, including any energy savings or releases during use.
  5. End-of-life management: Reuse, recycling, treatment or disposal of the product and its components.

A study that covers raw-material acquisition through end-of-life disposal is often described as a cradle-to-grave assessment. A narrower study may examine only selected stages, but its boundaries must be stated.

Four main phases of LCA

The international LCA framework identifies 4 related phases.

1. Goal and scope definition

The study specifies what is being compared, why the comparison is made and which processes are included.

For example, 2 water-treatment technologies should be compared for an equivalent treatment function. Comparing unrelated quantities of equipment would not provide a meaningful environmental comparison.

2. Life-cycle inventory analysis

The inventory identifies relevant inputs and outputs, such as material consumption, energy use, water consumption, emissions and waste associated with the defined system.

3. Life-cycle impact assessment

Inventory information is used to evaluate categories of potential environmental impact, such as climate-related effects and resource use.

4. Interpretation

The findings are examined to identify important impacts, limitations and conclusions consistent with the study's goal and scope.

How LCA differs from nanotoxicology

Nanotoxicology examines possible harmful biological effects of nanomaterials. Life-cycle assessment examines the wider potential environmental impacts of products and processes across defined stages.

The 2 approaches are complementary but not interchangeable. A product may have a comparatively low carbon footprint while still requiring careful assessment of a particular toxic exposure. Similarly, a material with low toxicity during ordinary use may require substantial energy during manufacture.

Environmental impact categories and trade-offs

Possible trade-offs include:

  • Reduced electricity use during operation versus greater energy use during manufacture.
  • Improved water purification versus production and disposal of spent treatment materials.
  • Longer product life versus difficulty separating nanoscale components during recycling.
  • Lower material consumption versus possible release of a harmful substance at end of life.

An environmentally preferable product should be identified using a comparison that covers the relevant function, life-cycle stages and impacts rather than relying only on a single benefit.

International standards for LCA

ISO 14040:2006, titled Environmental Management — Life Cycle Assessment — Principles and Framework, describes the overall LCA framework.

ISO 14044:2006, titled Environmental Management — Life Cycle Assessment — Requirements and Guidelines, provides requirements and guidance for conducting LCA studies.

Both editions were listed by the International Organization for Standardization as published and confirmed in 2022, with applicable amendments, at the content cutoff of 13 November 2026.

ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 are environmental assessment standards. Following an LCA standard does not, by itself, prove that a nanomedicine is clinically safe or that a nanofertiliser is legally authorised for sale.

Prelims focus

  • LCA stands for life-cycle assessment.
  • Cradle-to-grave assessment extends from raw-material acquisition to end-of-life management.
  • The 4 LCA phases are goal and scope definition, inventory analysis, impact assessment and interpretation.
  • ISO 14040:2006 describes LCA principles and framework.
  • ISO 14044:2006 provides LCA requirements and guidelines.
  • Trap: Low environmental impact over a product's life cycle does not automatically establish low toxicological risk in every exposure situation.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 164-168; International Organization for Standardization, ISO 14040:2006, Environmental Management — Life Cycle Assessment — Principles and Framework, abstract and status record; ISO 14044:2006, Environmental Management — Life Cycle Assessment — Requirements and Guidelines, abstract and status record; ISO records consulted 13 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Five stages run from raw-material acquisition to end-of-life management, with possible environmental burdens linked to every stage.
pictures.caption: Life-cycle assessment considers burdens before, during and after product use.

pictures.alt: The 4 LCA phases connect environmental comparison with interpretation, alongside the roles of ISO 14040:2006 and ISO 14044:2006.
pictures.caption: The 4 LCA phases organise environmental comparison and interpretation.

title: Life-Cycle Assessment and Sustainable Nanotechnology

body:
Why does nanotechnology need governance?

Governance refers to the institutions, rules, standards and procedures that guide how a technology is developed, evaluated, introduced and monitored.

Nanotechnology is used across medicines, agriculture, industrial materials, electronics and environmental treatment. These applications have different purposes and risks. Therefore, scientific research programmes, product-specific regulations, technical standards and workplace-safety recommendations must be distinguished.

India's National Mission on Nano Science and Technology

The Government of India approved the National Mission on Nano Science and Technology, commonly known as the Nano Mission, on 3 May 2007.

The mission was associated with the Department of Science and Technology (DST) and supported India's capacity in nanoscience and nanotechnology.

Its broad purposes included encouraging research, developing scientific infrastructure, supporting trained personnel and promoting useful applications.

A research mission helps develop scientific capabilities. It does not automatically grant permission to market every product that uses nanotechnology.

Medical evaluation in India

The Guidelines for Evaluation of Nanopharmaceuticals in India were issued in October 2019 by the Department of Biotechnology, Indian Council of Medical Research and Central Drugs Standard Control Organization.

These guidelines address scientific matters relevant to nanopharmaceutical evaluation, including product characterisation, quality, safety and effectiveness.

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) is India's central drug regulatory organisation. Applicable drug laws and rules govern authorisation. The 2019 scientific guidelines should not be mistaken for a blanket approval of nanopharmaceutical products.

Regulation of nanofertilisers in India

The Fertiliser (Control) Order, 1985, is relevant to the regulation of specified fertiliser products.

According to the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers' official statement of 6 August 2024, Nano DAP had been notified under the Fertiliser (Control) Order following bio-efficacy trials and toxicology tests.

That statement also reported permissions for specified manufacturers and preliminary crop trials indicating the possibility of saving some granular DAP. It did not establish universal replacement of all conventional DAP.

This is an example of product-specific regulatory evaluation, which is different from funding basic nanoscience research.

Gujarat's identifiable application

The IFFCO Nano Urea (Liquid) Plant at Kalol, Gujarat, was inaugurated on 28 May 2022. It provides a concrete example of nano-based agricultural manufacturing in the state.

The Kalol event is a manufacturing milestone. It is separate from the national Nano Mission's 2007 approval and the 2019 medical evaluation guidelines.

International standards and safety guidance

ISO/TC 229 and nanotechnology vocabulary

The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) develops international standards through technical committees. ISO/TC 229 deals with nanotechnologies, including terminology and related technical matters.

ISO 80004-1:2023, titled Nanotechnologies — Vocabulary — Part 1: Core Vocabulary, defines core nanotechnology terms to support consistent communication.

According to ISO's published record, this standard was issued in July 2023 and remained listed as published at the cutoff of 13 November 2026.

WHO worker-protection guidelines

The World Health Organization (WHO) issued guidelines on protecting workers from potential risks of manufactured nanomaterials on 2 February 2017.

These guidelines provide occupational-health recommendations, especially concerning assessment and control of inhalation exposure. They are not an Indian statute or a product-marketing approval.

European regulatory example

In the European Union, the REACH framework addresses the registration, evaluation, authorisation and restriction of chemicals. Specific requirements for nanoforms under REACH took effect on 1 January 2020.

This illustrates how an existing chemical-regulatory framework can include requirements for nanoscale forms. It does not mean that all nanomaterials are banned or that the European requirements automatically operate as Indian law.

Standards, guidance and enforceable regulation

InstrumentMain purposeImportant distinction
DST Nano MissionResearch and capacity-building supportNot product approval
India's 2019 nanopharmaceutical guidelinesScientific evaluation frameworkDo not replace applicable drug-approval law
Fertiliser (Control) Order, 1985Regulation of specified fertilisersProduct-specific legal framework
ISO nanotechnology standardsConsistent terminology and technical methodsNot automatically statutory Indian law
WHO 2017 guidelinesWorker-health recommendationsNot a marketing authorisation

Voluntary technical standards can become legally relevant when adopted or incorporated into applicable rules or contractual requirements. Their status must therefore be understood in the specific regulatory context.

Responsible development: connecting the entire subtopic

Responsible nanotechnology requires 3 related judgements. First, the material must perform its intended function, such as drug delivery, sensing or pollutant removal. Second, its potential human and environmental effects must be understood under realistic exposure conditions. Third, the product must meet the applicable evaluation, safety and regulatory requirements.

A successful demonstration of technical performance is not sufficient evidence of safety or legal authorisation. Likewise, scientific uncertainty requires careful evaluation rather than an automatic assumption that all nanotechnology is harmful.

Prelims focus

  • The National Mission on Nano Science and Technology was approved on 3 May 2007 and is associated with DST.
  • India's Guidelines for Evaluation of Nanopharmaceuticals were issued in October 2019.
  • The IFFCO Nano Urea (Liquid) Plant at Kalol, Gujarat, was inaugurated on 28 May 2022.
  • The Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers reported Nano DAP's notification under the Fertiliser (Control) Order, 1985, on 6 August 2024.
  • ISO/TC 229 concerns nanotechnologies; ISO 80004-1:2023 concerns core vocabulary.
  • WHO's worker-protection guidelines date from 2017, while explicit EU REACH nanoform requirements began on 1 January 2020.
  • Trap: A research programme, an international standard, a scientific guideline and a legally enforceable product regulation are not interchangeable.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Department of Science and Technology, National Mission on Nano Science and Technology, record of 3 May 2007 approval; Government of India, Department of Biotechnology, Indian Council of Medical Research and Central Drugs Standard Control Organization, Guidelines for Evaluation of Nanopharmaceuticals in India, October 2019; Press Information Bureau, Prime Minister's Office, 28 May 2022, inauguration of IFFCO Nano Urea (Liquid) Plant at Kalol; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Government of India notifies Nano DAP under Fertilizer Control Order, 6 August 2024; International Organization for Standardization, ISO 80004-1:2023, publication and status record, July 2023; World Health Organization, WHO Guidelines on Protecting Workers from Potential Risks of Manufactured Nanomaterials, 2 February 2017; European Chemicals Agency, Nanomaterials, section on REACH nanoform requirements effective 1 January 2020; official sources consulted 13 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Indian nanotechnology milestones concern research, medical evaluation and agricultural production or regulation.

pictures.alt: Nanotechnology applications connect to distinct assessments of risk, environmental fate, life cycle and governance; performance alone does not establish safety or permission.
pictures.caption: Useful nanotechnology must be considered together with exposure, environmental effects and applicable governance.

title: Nanotechnology Governance, Standards and Indian Initiatives
